messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Multipliers
parts:
Barbara and List:

A glance at the Distance Users Manual discusses the topic of multipliers
in Chapter 8 (Conventional distance sampling). In the section entitled
"Additional uses of multipliers" the common/rare species use of
multipliers as you are describing is defined. You will note that the
model definition to use in fitting the detection function is the uniform
with no adjustment terms; and specify the multiplier in the Multiplier
tab. The detection function fitted by Distance will produce a
probability of detection of 1.0, and the estimated density will
incorporate the multiplier you specified.

By specifying a detection function model other than the uniform with no
adjustment term, you are defeating the purpose of providing your
multiplier. Because of the few detections of your rare species, you are
requesting that a detection function *not* be fit to the data for that
species, and the multiplier (and SE) you provide will perform the
function of specifying detectability.

I hope that helps clarify your dilemma.

messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: Re: Multipliers
parts:
Hi Barbara, list:

Further to Eric's message, in the online manual's program reference, under
Multipliers Tab - CDS and MCDS, is the text below. If you didn't find it then
other probably didn't either, so I've moved it to the Users Guide instead.

- Len

Aside: In fact, the Distance Analysis Engine only recognizes the multiply
operator - i.e., all multipliers multiply the density estimate. So, the
Distance Interface uses a little trick to pass multipliers to the Analysis
Engine when the operator is divide. To pass the multiplier value, it simply
takes 1 / multiplier value. To pass the multiplier SE, it takes SE /
(multiplier value * multiplier value). You can see this happening if you look
at the first page of the Analysis Details Results tab for an analysis that has
been run with multipliers, where the operator is a divider. About half-way
down the first page is a small table listing the multiplier values and SEs
used. If, for example, you used a multiplier with a value of 0.9 and an SE of
0.5, you'll see that the actual value passed in was 1.1 (i.e., 1 / 0.9) and
the SE was 0.6128 (i.e., 0.5 / (0.9*0.9) ).

--
